html:
Nahuatl is a language of the Uto-Aztecan family, spoken in central Mexico for well over a thousand years. It was the language of the Mexica of Tenochtitlan and of their Triple Alliance, and the common language of trade and rule across much of Mesoamerica.

Before the conquest it was written in pictures and glyphs, as in tribute lists like the Codex Mendoza. Poems, songs and speeches were learned by heart; some are credited to the poet-king Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco.

After 1521 Spanish friars such as the Twelve Apostles learned it to preach, and wrote it in the Latin alphabet. Some of the first books from the printing press in Mexico were in Nahuatl. Bernardino de Sahagún worked with Nahua scholars to record their world in it. Nahua towns kept records, wills and petitions in it for centuries.

Spanish slowly pushed it back, but about 1.5 million Nahua people still speak it, in places such as Guerrero, Puebla and Veracruz. Words such as chocolate, tomato, avocado, chili and coyote came into English from it through Spanish.
